course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 3
firstTopic.summary: How the Seven Years' War, British imperial reform, colonial self-government, and Enlightenment ideas set the stage for independence and the first experiments in republican government, 1754–1800.

topic.title: Continuity and Change in Period 3
topic.summary: A guide to describing and explaining what stayed the same and what changed in American politics, society, and ideas between 1754 and 1800.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a continuity in American government between 1754 and 1800?
choices: The Crown continued to appoint the governors of the states and to approve the laws that they passed
Colonial assemblies became state legislatures, and traditions of local self-government continued
Parliament continued to tax the states and to regulate their trade after the Treaty of Paris
Hereditary rulers continued to hold the highest offices in the national and state governments
questions.explanation: Colonists carried their experience of elected assemblies into the new state governments.
choiceExplanations: The Crown's authority over the states ended with independence.
Colonists carried their experience of elected assemblies into the new state governments.
Parliament's authority ended with independence.
The new governments were republics without hereditary rulers.
questions.distinguisher: The Crown-appoints choice is close because royal governors had been common in the colonies, but independence ended that practice.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a major change in American government between 1754 and 1800?
choices: Colonists who had been subjects of a monarch built republics with written constitutions
Colonists who had been governed by assemblies placed all power in the hands of a single executive
Colonists who had been governed by Parliament chose a permanent monarch to rule the new nation
Colonists who had held no elections began voting for their leaders for the first time in 1789
questions.explanation: The Revolution replaced rule by a king and Parliament with republican governments based on written constitutions.
choiceExplanations: The Revolution replaced rule by a king and Parliament with republican governments based on written constitutions.
States gave the most power to legislatures, and the Constitution divided power among three branches.
Americans rejected monarchy.
Colonists had elected their assemblies for generations.
questions.distinguisher: The single-executive choice is close because the Constitution created a president, but it divided power among three branches.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a continuity in American society from the colonial period to 1800?
choices: Slavery had ended in every state by 1800, as the Declaration of Independence had required
Women gained the right to vote in every state by 1800, because of their role in the Revolution
Property requirements for voting were abolished in every state by 1800, as republican ideals required
Slavery remained legal and grew in the South, despite the Revolution's ideals of liberty
questions.explanation: The Revolution inspired antislavery action in the North, yet slavery remained central to the Southern economy and grew with cotton.
choiceExplanations: Slavery continued in the South and the Declaration did not require its end.
Women could not vote in most states.
Property qualifications remained common.
The Revolution inspired antislavery action in the North, yet slavery remained central to the Southern economy and grew with cotton.
questions.distinguisher: The slavery-ended choice is close because the northern states did act, but slavery continued across the South.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would be the strongest claim about continuity and change in Period 3?
choices: The Revolution changed nothing, because the colonists already had governments and elected assemblies before independence began
The Revolution changed everything in American society, including the status of enslaved people, of women, and of Native nations
Independence changed the form of government, but slavery and property qualifications continued, limiting the Revolution's effects
The colonists were loyal to Britain until 1776, and then they suddenly became a united nation
questions.explanation: A strong claim names both the change and the continuity and explains the limits of change.
choiceExplanations: This overlooks changes such as republican government and the Constitution.
This overlooks the limits of the Revolution for enslaved people and women.
A strong claim names both the change and the continuity and explains the limits of change.
This overlooks the earlier colonial resistance and the later divisions within the new nation.
questions.distinguisher: The changed-nothing choice is close because some patterns continued, but it ignores the major changes in government.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following represents a continuity in voting in the states during the Revolutionary era?
choices: Voting was extended to all adult residents of the states, regardless of property or sex
Property requirements for voting remained common, and women could not vote in most states
Voting was limited to members of the established church in each state, as in the colonial period
Voting for members of Congress was controlled by the king, who appointed the Senate
questions.explanation: Republican ideals did not immediately produce universal suffrage, and property qualifications continued in most states.
choiceExplanations: Voting remained limited in most states.
Republican ideals did not immediately produce universal suffrage, and property qualifications continued in most states.
Many states ended religious tests and official churches.
Senators were chosen by state legislatures.
questions.distinguisher: The all-residents choice is close because the Revolution encouraged ideas of democracy, but voting rights remained limited.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a continuity in the experience of American Indians from 1754 to 1800?
choices: Native nations kept losing land as settlers moved west, and allied with outside powers to resist
Native nations gained control of the land east of the Appalachians through treaties with the Congress
Native nations avoided all conflict with settlers by moving to the Pacific coast in large numbers
Native nations became citizens of the United States with the right to vote after the Constitution
questions.explanation: Settlers continued to move into Native lands, from the Proclamation of 1763 through the Treaty of Greenville.
choiceExplanations: Settlers continued to move into Native lands, from the Proclamation of 1763 through the Treaty of Greenville.
Native nations lost land and did not gain control of the East.
Native nations resisted and fought to keep their lands.
Native people were not citizens under the Constitution.
questions.distinguisher: The land-gain choice is close because treaties were signed, but treaties more often transferred land to the United States.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a continuity in the international position of North America from 1754 to 1800?
choices: European powers withdrew from North America after 1763, which ended all disputes over borders
Spain and Britain became allies of the United States and ended their claims in North America
European powers remained in North America, which challenged the nation's borders and trade
France regained control of the Ohio Valley, which restored the French trade networks
questions.explanation: Europe remained a factor from the Seven Years' War through the 1790s, when the United States dealt with Britain and Spain on borders and with Britain and France on trade.
choiceExplanations: European powers remained present after 1763 and after 1783.
Spain and Britain kept claims and forts that created conflicts with the United States.
Europe remained a factor from the Seven Years' War through the 1790s, when the United States dealt with Britain and Spain on borders and with Britain and France on trade.
France gave up its claims east of the Mississippi in 1763.
questions.distinguisher: The withdrawal choice is close because France left the East, but Britain and Spain stayed.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why the Constitution of 1787 can be seen as both a change and a continuity?
choices: It ended the power of the states and restored a system in which a king chose the national officials
It copied the Articles of Confederation without any changes in the structure or powers of the government
It gave all power to the Congress and eliminated both the president and the national courts
It strengthened the national government while keeping republican government and separated powers
questions.explanation: The Constitution changed the structure and powers of the national government, while it preserved republican principles and limits on power.
choiceExplanations: The Constitution kept the states and rejected monarchy.
The Constitution changed the structure and powers of the national government.
The Constitution created a president and a national court system.
The Constitution changed the structure and powers of the national government, while it preserved republican principles and limits on power.
questions.distinguisher: The copied-Articles choice is close because the Constitution kept some features, but it made important changes.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why the American independence movement had effects on society beyond politics?
choices: British officials required the new states to reform their societies as a condition of the peace treaty of 1783
Revolutionary ideals of liberty and equality led people to question slavery and inherited privilege
The Constitution required the states to adopt laws ending slavery and giving women the vote
The war ended all inequalities, and the new nation therefore needed no further reforms
questions.explanation: The language of the Revolution encouraged groups to ask whether its ideals applied to them.
choiceExplanations: The treaty did not require social reforms.
The language of the Revolution encouraged groups to ask whether its ideals applied to them.
The Constitution did not require these changes.
Many inequalities continued after the war.
questions.distinguisher: The Constitution choice is close because it shaped later reforms, but it did not require these changes.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.
